examples: The board affirmed that no layoffs were planned for the coming year.
She quietly affirmed her belief that the study would hold up.
The witness chose to affirm rather than swear on a Bible.
The appeals court affirmed the conviction in a two-page order.
The ambassador affirmed to reporters that the treaty remained in force.
In his letter he affirmed that the money had been repaid in full.
Nobody at the hearing affirmed that the deadline was still in force.
entries.русский: утверждать, подтверждать — официально повторять свою позицию; юр. заявлять без присяги
entries.type: reporting verb — statement, formally and deliberately restated
entries.patterns: affirm + that-clause · affirm + noun phrase · affirm + to sb + that-clause · affirm (intransitive, in court: he affirmed rather than swore)
entries.never: affirm someone that and affirm to do something. There is no personal object and no infinitive complement: ✗ He affirmed us that the funding was secure, ✗ She affirmed to support the measure. The addressee, if you need one, takes to. Repairs: affirmed that the funding was secure, affirmed to the committee that the funding was secure, affirmed her support for the measure, or — if the point is settling someone's doubt rather than stating for the record — assured us that the funding was secure.
entries.reports: a public, deliberate statement that something is true, usually restating a position already on record. Unlike claim, it carries no doubt; unlike confirm, it does not require a prior question. Two specialized senses live alongside it: to affirm in court is to make a solemn declaration in place of an oath (He affirmed rather than swore), and an appellate court affirms a lower court's ruling by letting it stand.

examples: Prosecutors allege that the payments were routed through three shell companies.
The suit alleges a pattern of retaliation going back four years.
She is alleged to have signed the forms without reading them.
None of the alleged victims has been named publicly.
The article carefully alleged nothing it could not document.
He allegedly left the building twenty minutes before the alarm sounded.
entries.русский: утверждать без доказательств — юр./газетн. обвинять, не ручаясь за правдивость
entries.type: reporting verb — accusation asserted but unproven
entries.patterns: allege + that-clause · allege + noun phrase · be alleged + to-infinitive (passive) · allege + sb + to be (rare, legal)
entries.never: allege to do something in the active voice — ✗ He alleged to have seen the car. The infinitive frame exists only in the passive: ✓ He is alleged to have seen the car. Also ✗ allege someone something and ✗ allege sb that: ✗ She alleged the police that he had lied → ✓ She alleged that he had lied.
entries.reports: the strongest doubt marker in English, and the only one that also carries an accusation. Allege tells the reader two things at once: the statement is unproven, and it charges someone with wrongdoing. This is exactly why journalists reach for it — writing the company allegedly falsified the invoices reports the accusation without the newspaper adopting it. Use it for wrongdoing only; she alleged that the train was late is comic, because nothing is at stake.

examples: The mayor announced that the pool would reopen in June.
They announced the merger an hour before the market opened.
She walked in and announced to nobody in particular that the elevator was broken.
The airline has not yet announced which routes it will cut.
He announced his resignation in a two-sentence email.
Nothing was announced about the second round of funding.
entries.русский: объявлять, сообщать — публично оглашать новость, обычно впервые
entries.type: reporting verb — public statement of news
entries.patterns: announce + that-clause · announce + noun phrase · announce + wh-clause · announce + to sb + that-clause · announce + noun phrase + to sb
entries.never: announce someone something and announce someone that. Announce is not ditransitive; the addressee needs to: ✗ She announced us the results → ✓ She announced the results to us / announced to us that the results were in. Also ✗ announce to do.
entries.reports: making something publicly known, usually for the first time. It presupposes both that the content is true and that it is news — which is why he announced that he was tired sounds like a joke. Compared with declare it is plainer and less ceremonial; compared with proclaim it lacks any grandeur.

examples: She argues that the second experiment was never properly controlled.
The defense argued the case for four days.
He argued against expanding the program until the audit was finished.
They argued her into taking the job by promising a relocation budget.
The two of them argued about whether to sell the house.
It could be argued that the whole policy was obsolete by the time it passed.
entries.русский: доказывать, утверждать с доводами — отстаивать позицию, приводя основания
entries.type: reporting verb — a claim advanced with reasons
entries.patterns: argue + that-clause · argue + for/against + noun phrase / -ing · argue + noun phrase (argue a case, argue a point) · argue + sb + into/out of + -ing · argue + about/over + noun phrase / wh-clause (quarrel sense) · argue + with sb (+ about sth)
entries.never: argue someone that and argue to do something — ✗ He argued me that the plan was risky, ✗ She argued to raise the fee. Repairs: argued that the plan was risky, argued for raising the fee. And note that the persuasion frame requires a preposition: ✗ He argued me to stay → ✓ He argued me into staying.
entries.reports: asserting a position together with the reasons for it. The verb commits the speaker to a supporting case, so it presupposes that the point is contestable — which is why it is the default verb of academic writing (Ellison argues that…) but sounds combative in a report of casual conversation. It does not signal doubt the way claim does; it signals contested ground.

examples: The report asserts that the software was never tested on live data.
She asserted her right to have a lawyer present.
He asserted, without producing a single document, that the deal had been approved.
The company has asserted control over three of the four subsidiaries.
In meetings she has learned to assert herself early.
Nobody in the room asserted anything they could not back up.
entries.русский: заявлять, утверждать — категорично и уверенно, обычно без доказательств
entries.type: reporting verb — statement made forcefully and without hedging
entries.patterns: assert + that-clause · assert + noun phrase (assert a right, assert control) · assert + oneself
entries.never: assert someone that, assert someone something, assert to do something, and assert someone to do something. ✗ He asserted the committee that the figures were sound, ✗ She asserted to know the answer, ✗ They asserted him to have signed the form. Repairs: asserted that the figures were sound, claimed to know the answer, asserted that he had signed the form.
entries.reports: stating something as fact, flatly and with confidence, and usually without offering support. That last part is what gives assert its faint edge in journalism: by drawing attention to the confidence rather than the evidence, it invites the reader to notice that nothing was proved. It is a milder doubt marker than claim — closer to neutral — but it is not fully neutral, and he asserted in a news story is rarely a compliment.

examples: The nurse assured him that the swelling would go down in a day or two.
She assured us of her support before the vote was even scheduled.
I can assure you that nobody here saw the email.
He assured the landlord the rent would clear by Friday.
Rest assured — the file was backed up before the crash.
The contractor assured them repeatedly, and then missed the deadline anyway.
entries.русский: заверять, уверять кого-л. — обязательно с адресатом: заверяют всегда кого-то
entries.type: reporting verb — statement made to remove someone's doubt
entries.patterns: assure + sb + that-clause · assure + sb + of + noun phrase · assure + sb (alone)
entries.never: assure that with no object. This is the single commonest error with the verb: ✗ He assured that the parts would arrive Friday. Assure is obligatorily ditransitive — somebody has to be reassured. Repairs: assured us that the parts would arrive, or drop the verb for a neutral one: said that the parts would arrive. Also ✗ assure to sb that, ✗ assure sb to do (that is promise or urge).
entries.reports: telling someone directly that something is true, in order to settle their doubt. Where affirm is oriented toward the record, assure is oriented toward the addressee — the point is the listener's peace of mind, not the public statement. It carries no doubt of its own, but the writer's he assured us often invites the reader to notice that the assurance may not have held.

examples: Two colleagues attested that he had been in the building all morning.
Anyone who has waited in that line can attest to how slow it is.
A notary must attest the signature before the deed is filed.
The scorch marks on the ceiling attest to an earlier fire.
She attested under penalty of perjury that the return was complete.
Nothing in the file attests to a second inspection.
entries.русский: свидетельствовать, удостоверять — подтверждать по личному знанию; юр. заверять
entries.type: reporting verb — formal statement from firsthand knowledge
entries.patterns: attest + that-clause · attest + to + noun phrase / -ing / wh-clause · attest + noun phrase (attest a signature, attest a will)
entries.never: attest to + a that-clause. The preposition takes a noun phrase, an -ing form, or a wh-clause — but never a bare that-clause: ✗ She attested to that the copy was genuine. Repairs: attested that the copy was genuine, or attested to the authenticity of the copy, or the idiom attested to the fact that the copy was genuine. Also ✗ attest someone that and ✗ attest to do.
entries.reports: bearing witness — asserting something on the strength of one's own knowledge, usually in a setting where the statement counts for something. It presupposes the speaker's credibility rather than the truth of the content, which is why an inanimate subject works so naturally: the wear on the steps attests to a century of use.

examples: The complaint avers that the contract was signed under duress.
He averred, with a straight face, that he had read every page.
She averred her innocence in the same flat tone all afternoon.
Counsel must aver the facts supporting jurisdiction in the opening paragraphs.
In the memoir he avers that the letter was destroyed by accident.
Nobody in the deposition averred anything about a second meeting.
entries.русский: книжн./юр. утверждать, заявлять — в обычной речи звучит устарело и вычурно
entries.register: formal; legal, literary, rare in speech
entries.type: reporting verb — statement made positively and on the record
entries.patterns: aver + that-clause · aver + noun phrase (legal: aver facts in a pleading)
entries.never: aver someone that and aver to do something — ✗ He averred the court that he had paid, ✗ She averred to have paid. Repairs: averred that he had paid, claimed to have paid.
entries.reports: stating something confidently and formally, and in legal pleading, alleging a fact one intends to prove at trial. Outside of court filings and self-consciously literary prose it reads as precious or archaic — he averred in ordinary American writing sounds like a nineteenth-century novel. Say said, insisted, or asserted instead unless the register genuinely calls for it.

examples: She avowed that her only interest in the case was the principle.
He publicly avowed his support for the boycott a week before the vote.
An avowed skeptic, she read the whole report twice before commenting.
The senator avowed himself satisfied with the compromise.
The company disavowed the memo within hours of its leaking.
Few of them would avow in writing what they said freely in the hallway.
entries.русский: книжн. открыто признавать — заявлять о взглядах или верности, которые можно было бы скрыть
entries.type: reporting verb — open admission of a belief or allegiance
entries.patterns: avow + that-clause · avow + noun phrase · avow + oneself + noun phrase / adjective (avowed himself satisfied)
entries.never: avow someone that and avow to do something — ✗ He avowed us that he had voted for it, ✗ She avowed to resign. Repairs: avowed that he had voted for it, vowed to resign (a different verb, and a different act).
entries.reports: declaring openly something one might reasonably be expected to conceal — a belief, a loyalty, a motive. It presupposes candor and a small cost to the speaker. The past participle is far commoner than the finite verb: an avowed socialist, her avowed aim. Its opposite, disavow, denies any connection: the campaign disavowed the flyer.

examples: He claims the fence was already down when he got there.
She claimed to have no memory of the conversation.
Two different groups have claimed responsibility for the outage.
The label claims the bottle contains no added sugar.
Nobody has claimed the bag left in the lobby.
They claimed a deduction that the auditor immediately disallowed.
entries.русский: утверждать, заявлять — маркер сомнения: автор за сказанное не ручается («якобы»)
entries.type: reporting verb — statement the writer does not endorse
entries.patterns: claim + that-clause · claim + to-infinitive (same subject) · claim + noun phrase · claim + sb/sth + to be (formal, rare)
entries.never: claim someone to do something and claim someone that. ✗ He claimed me to be lying, ✗ She claimed us that the package had shipped. Claim takes no indirect object and no object-controlled infinitive. Repairs: claimed that I was lying, told us that the package had shipped.
entries.control: claim + to-infinitive is same-subject only. He claimed to have paid means he paid. To report a claim about somebody else you need the that-clause: He claimed that his brother had paid — never ✗ He claimed his brother to have paid. The one apparent exception is the formal claim + object + to be frame in the Patterns line (the report claimed the signature to be a forgery): it is restricted to to be plus a complement, it is confined to legal and academic prose, and a learner is always safe rewriting it as a that-clause. No other infinitive is available after an object.
entries.reports: the everyday doubt marker of English. Writing he claimed he was home tells the reader, in one word, that the writer is not vouching for it. That is a real editorial act, not a stylistic flourish: said is neutral, pointed out endorses, claimed withholds. Unlike allege, it does not accuse anyone; unlike purport, it takes a human subject comfortably.

examples: The lab confirmed that the sample was contaminated.
Can you confirm whether the room is still available for Thursday?
He confirmed the appointment by text an hour beforehand.
Two sources have confirmed to the paper that the talks broke down.
The species was later confirmed to be new to science.
Nobody at the agency would confirm who had signed off on the waiver.
entries.русский: подтверждать — сообщать, что предполагавшееся верно; автор с этим согласен
entries.type: reporting verb — statement verifying something already in question
entries.patterns: confirm + that-clause · confirm + noun phrase · confirm + wh-clause · confirm + to sb + that-clause · be confirmed + to-infinitive (passive)
entries.never: confirm someone that — ✗ She confirmed me that the meeting was on. The addressee needs to: ✓ She confirmed to me that the meeting was on, or simply She confirmed that the meeting was on. Also ✗ confirm to do.
entries.reports: stating that something already suggested, rumored, or asked about is in fact true. It is factive — He confirmed that the deal had collapsed commits the writer to the collapse, which is why a newspaper will not use it for a statement it cannot stand behind. It also presupposes a prior question; there is nothing to confirm if nobody wondered.

examples: The defense contends that the search was unlawful from the start.
Critics contend the model breaks down at low temperatures.
He contended that no one had ever explained the fee to him.
Both sides contend that the other walked away from the table.
She has contended for years that the surveys undercount renters.
It has been contended, though never demonstrated, that the two events are linked.
entries.русский: утверждать, доказывать — отстаивать позицию в споре, где есть другая сторона
entries.type: reporting verb — a claim advanced inside a dispute
entries.patterns: contend + that-clause · contend + with + noun phrase (a different sense: cope with) · contend + for + noun phrase (a different sense: compete for)
entries.never: contend someone that, contend to do something, and — in the reporting sense — contend + noun phrase. ✗ He contended his innocence → ✓ He contended that he was innocent or asserted his innocence. ✗ The union contended the company to be at fault → ✓ contended that the company was at fault.
entries.reports: asserting a position in an argument that has another side. Contend presupposes an opponent, which is why it belongs to court reporting, academic disagreement, and news coverage of disputes. It carries a mild doubt tint — the writer is describing one party's position, not the facts — but it is more dignified than claim and does not accuse anyone.

examples: The governor declared a state of emergency before the storm made landfall.
He declared that the numbers had been checked twice.
The judge declared the contract unenforceable.
She declared herself satisfied and went home.
You have to declare anything over ten thousand dollars at customs.
Two senators have declared against the bill in its current form.
entries.русский: объявлять, провозглашать — официально и авторитетно, нередко перформативно
entries.type: reporting verb — formal public statement made with authority
entries.patterns: declare + that-clause · declare + noun phrase · declare + sb/sth + (to be) + complement (declared the election invalid) · declare + oneself + adjective / noun phrase (declared herself satisfied, declared himself a candidate) · declare + to sb + that-clause · declare + for/against + noun phrase
entries.never: declare someone that and declare someone something — ✗ He declared us that the meeting was over, ✗ She declared me the results. Repairs: declared to us that the meeting was over, announced the results to me. Also ✗ declare to do.
entries.reports: stating something formally and with standing, often in a way that makes it so — I declare this meeting adjourned does not describe an adjournment, it performs one. On the doubt scale it is neutral as to truth but loud as to manner, and in ordinary narrative it lends a whiff of theater: she declared that she was finished with the whole thing.

examples: She emphasized that the results were preliminary.
The coach emphasized footwork all through the first week.
He emphasized how little time was left before the filing date.
The memo emphasized to managers that overtime had to be approved in advance.
Every speaker emphasized the same three numbers.
It cannot be emphasized enough that the backup runs only on weekdays.
entries.русский: подчёркивать, особо отмечать — придавать уже сказанному дополнительный вес
entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.patterns: emphasize + that-clause · emphasize + noun phrase · emphasize + wh-clause · emphasize + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: emphasize on — the commonest error with this verb, imported from the noun. The noun takes on (put emphasis on the deadline); the verb takes a plain direct object: ✗ He emphasized on the deadline → ✓ He emphasized the deadline. Also ✗ emphasize someone that (✗ She emphasized me that it was urgent → ✓ emphasized to me that it was urgent) and ✗ emphasize to do.
entries.spelling: American English writes -ize. Emphasise is British and has no place in American copy — see spelling the reporting verbs.
entries.reports: not a new claim but extra weight on part of one. It is factive: she emphasized that the deadline was firm commits the writer to the deadline being firm. Compared with insist it implies no resistance; the speaker is underlining, not defending.

examples: Most economists hold that the effect is too small to measure.
The Ninth Circuit held that the ordinance violated the First Amendment.
She holds the view that the whole department should be restructured.
It is widely held that the practice began in the 1930s.
He held the study to be worthless and said so in print.
Nobody now holds that the two species are closely related.
entries.русский: держаться мнения, считать; юр. постановлять — суд формулирует правовую позицию
entries.type: reporting verb — a settled belief, or a court's binding ruling
entries.patterns: hold + that-clause · hold + sb/sth + (to be) + complement (held the clause to be void) · hold + noun phrase (hold the view, hold an opinion) · it is held + that-clause (passive, very common)
entries.never: hold someone that and hold to do something — ✗ He held the jury that the statute applied, ✗ The court held to reverse the judgment. Repairs: held that the statute applied, voted to reverse the judgment.
entries.reports: maintaining a position one is settled in rather than arguing toward — a standing belief, a doctrine, or, in law, the part of a decision that binds later courts. Keep the legal pair straight: a court holds the law (the court held that the search was unlawful) and finds the facts (the court found that the officer had entered at 9 p.m.).

entries.meaning: Two consequences worth memorizing. The negative is a bare not in front of the verb — no do, no agreement: ✓ insisted that she not be told, ✗ that she doesn't be told, ✗ that she not is told. And the subjunctive is invisible except in the third-person singular and with be, so they insisted that we leave gives no clue which reading is intended; only that he leave and that it be filed show their hand. The same pattern runs after demand, require, request, recommend, propose, urge, ask, and stipulate, and after it is essential / vital / imperative that — the full treatment is in the mandative subjunctive. ---
examples: He insisted that the door had been locked when he left.
She insisted that the report be circulated before the meeting, not after.
They insisted on paying for dinner.
The landlord insisted on our signing a two-year lease.
I said no twice, and he insisted anyway.
The union insisted that no one be laid off before the arbitration was finished.
She insists she never received the second notice.
entries.русский: настаивать — упорно утверждать вопреки возражениям; либо требовать, не принимая отказа
entries.type: reporting verb — two acts under one word: a statement held against resistance, and a demand
entries.patterns: insist + that-clause (indicative = claim; bare subjunctive = demand) · insist + on/upon + noun phrase · insist + on/upon + -ing · insist + on/upon + sb + -ing · insist (intransitive)
entries.never: insist someone to do something — ✗ She insisted me to stay. This is the classic error, and insist blocks every part of it: no personal object, no infinitive, no object-controlled complement. Also ✗ insist to do, ✗ insist sb that, and ✗ insist doing — the -ing form is never bare, it always needs on: ✗ She insisted paying → ✓ She insisted on paying. Repairs: insisted that I stay, insisted on my staying, insisted on me staying (both possessive and object forms are current; the possessive is the more formal).
entries.subjunctive: this is the verb the mandative subjunctive was built for, and the mood you choose decides which speech act you are reporting. In the demand sense American English puts a bare base form in the that-clause — no -s, no to, no should — and because a bare form has no tense, reporting leaves it untouched. In the claim sense the clause is an ordinary tensed one and backshifts normally.
entries.reports: in the claim sense, continuing to assert something against doubt or contradiction — a soft signal that the hearer may not be buying it. In the demand sense, refusing to accept any alternative. Decide which act the speaker performed before you choose the mood.
entries.see also: maintain, stress, contend, stipulate, protest, recommend

examples: He has maintained from the first day that the account was not his.
She maintained her innocence through two trials.
The company maintains that the recall was voluntary.
Both witnesses maintained that the light had been green.
He maintained this position long after his own lawyers gave up on it.
They maintain, against all the evidence, that the map is accurate.
entries.русский: продолжать утверждать, стоять на своём — вопреки уже высказанным возражениям
entries.type: reporting verb — statement held to under pressure
entries.patterns: maintain + that-clause · maintain + noun phrase (maintain one's innocence, maintain a position)
entries.never: maintain someone that and maintain to do something — ✗ He maintained the police that he was home, ✗ She maintained to be innocent. Repairs: maintained that he was home, maintained her innocence / claimed to be innocent.
entries.reports: continuing to assert something in the face of contradiction. Maintain presupposes a challenge already made — the word itself says the position is under attack — so it is a soft doubt marker: the reader infers that somebody credible disagrees. Compare insist, which adds force and impatience, and contend, which places the statement inside a formal dispute.

examples: The foundation pledged four million dollars over three years.
Both candidates pledged to release ten years of tax returns.
She pledged that no employee would lose health coverage in the transition.
He pledged them his full support and then missed every meeting.
The signatories pledged themselves to a common set of standards.
Donors have pledged more than they have actually paid.
entries.русский: обязываться, торжественно обещать — публично и официально, чаще об организациях
entries.type: reporting verb — formal public commitment
entries.patterns: pledge + to-infinitive · pledge + that-clause · pledge + noun phrase · pledge + sb + noun phrase (pledged them his support) · pledge + to sb + that-clause · pledge + oneself + to + noun phrase / -ing
entries.never: pledge someone to do something in the sense "promise them that you will" — ✗ He pledged us to fix the road. That frame exists but means the opposite: pledge sb to sth binds the other person (she pledged them to secrecy). Nor is there a ditransitive that-clause: ✗ He pledged us that he would fix the road — the addressee needs to. Repairs: pledged to fix the road, pledged to us that he would fix the road, or promised us that he would fix the road. The only noun the addressee can carry directly is a thing pledged, not a clause: ✓ pledged them his support.
entries.reports: a formal, usually public promise, generally with money, policy, or institutional weight attached. Weaker as a personal oath than vow, and less solemn than swear — a government pledges, a person vows. It presupposes an audience: pledges are made where they can be counted.

examples: The paper posits that language learning and music share a single mechanism.
Let's posit a reader who has never seen the earlier draft.
She posited an intermediate stage that nobody has yet observed.
Critics say the model posits far more structure than the data support.
He posited that the two outbreaks had a common source, then set out to test it.
Nothing in the theory posits a hard limit on the number of participants.
entries.русский: науч. допускать, класть в основу — выдвигать посылку, не утверждая её истинности
entries.type: reporting verb — a claim put forward as a starting assumption
entries.patterns: posit + that-clause · posit + noun phrase
entries.never: posit someone that, posit to do something, and posit about. ✗ She posited us that the effect was real, ✗ He posited about a third mechanism. Repairs: posited that the effect was real, posited a third mechanism.
entries.reports: advancing a proposition as a premise, for the sake of argument, without asserting that it is true. It is the lowest-commitment verb in this file: let us posit that the market is efficient concedes nothing about actual markets. This makes it useless for reporting ordinary speech — nobody posits anything at dinner — and indispensable in academic writing.

examples: Mendel postulated particles of inheritance long before anyone saw a chromosome.
The theory postulates that the two populations were separated for ten thousand years.
She postulated an unobserved intermediate to make the numbers work.
Nothing in the argument requires us to postulate a designer.
He postulated that memory consolidation happens mostly during sleep.
Every one of the postulates was later shown to be unnecessary.
entries.русский: постулировать — принимать без доказательств как основу дальнейших рассуждений
entries.type: reporting verb — a claim asserted without proof, as a basis for reasoning
entries.patterns: postulate + that-clause · postulate + noun phrase
entries.never: postulate someone that and postulate to do something — ✗ He postulated us that the gene was duplicated, ✗ She postulated to explain the gap. Repairs: postulated that the gene had been duplicated, postulated a mechanism to explain the gap.
entries.reports: asserting something as true without evidence, in order to build on it. Slightly more committed than posit — a postulate is something you intend to keep, not merely to try out — and much more committed than hypothesize, which invites a test. The vowel of the last syllable is the only thing separating the verb from the noun: scientists postulate /leɪt/ a mechanism, and the postulate /lət/ is what they end up with.

examples: The governor proclaimed the first Monday in May a day of remembrance.
She proclaimed that the era of cheap money was over.
He proclaimed himself an expert after reading two articles.
The banner proclaimed a grand reopening that never happened.
Every review proclaimed the album a masterpiece.
Nobody was ready to proclaim victory with a third of the votes uncounted.
entries.русский: провозглашать — громко и торжественно; в современной прозе часто с иронией
entries.type: reporting verb — loud, public, ceremonial declaration
entries.patterns: proclaim + that-clause · proclaim + noun phrase · proclaim + sb/sth + (to be) + complement (proclaimed himself president) · proclaim + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: proclaim someone that — ✗ He proclaimed us that the war was over. Repairs: proclaimed to us that the war was over, or announced that the war was over. Also ✗ proclaim to do.
entries.reports: announcing publicly and grandly, with more ceremony than declare and far more than announce. In modern American prose it is very often ironic: he proclaimed the redesign a triumph signals that the writer does not agree. Used straight, it belongs to proclamations, coronations, and headlines.

examples: He professes to know nothing about how the money moved.
She professed a lifelong love of opera and then fell asleep in the second act.
Both candidates profess deep concern about the deficit.
The company professes that its supply chain is fully audited.
He professed himself shocked, which fooled nobody.
She professed her innocence in a two-page letter to the editor.
entries.русский: книжн. заявлять о своих взглядах, чувствах, умениях — часто с недоверием автора
entries.type: reporting verb — an open claim about one's own beliefs, feelings, or abilities
entries.patterns: profess + to-infinitive (same subject; especially profess to be) · profess + that-clause · profess + noun phrase (professed his innocence) · profess + oneself + adjective / noun phrase (professed himself satisfied, professed herself a convert)
entries.never: profess someone to do something and profess someone that — ✗ He professed her to be innocent, ✗ She professed us that she knew nothing. The infinitive is same-subject only. Repairs: professed that she was innocent, professed to know nothing.
entries.reports: claiming openly to hold a belief, feel a feeling, or possess a skill — and with the to-infinitive, the writer is almost always signaling skepticism. He professes to care about the neighborhood invites the reader to doubt that he does; he says he cares does not. That built-in eyebrow is the difference between profess and avow, which presupposes candor.

examples: She was pronounced dead at the scene.
The critic tasted three of them and pronounced the second one best.
The court will pronounce sentence on Thursday morning.
He declined to pronounce on a case still under appeal.
The inspector pronounced the wiring safe and signed the form.
Nobody has pronounced the project finished, but nobody is working on it either.
entries.русский: выносить вердикт, официально объявлять — решение действует в силу статуса говорящего
entries.type: reporting verb — an authoritative verdict
entries.patterns: pronounce + sb/sth + complement (pronounced the patient dead) · pronounce + that-clause · pronounce + on/upon + noun phrase · pronounce + noun phrase (pronounce sentence, pronounce judgment)
entries.never: pronounce someone that and pronounce to do something — ✗ The judge pronounced the jury that the trial was over, ✗ He pronounced to be satisfied. Repairs: told the jury that the trial was over, pronounced himself satisfied.
entries.reports: delivering a judgment that is official because of who is delivering it. The verdict frame — pronounce + object + complement — is the core one, and it is performative: a doctor's I pronounce him dead creates the legal fact. Used of ordinary opinions it is deliberately grand, and usually a little arch: she tasted it and pronounced it edible. The other pronounce — saying a word aloud — is the same word and is covered in Pronunciation.

examples: He protested that the charge had never appeared on any statement he received.
She protested her innocence loudly enough for the whole floor to hear.
Hundreds protested the closure outside the district office.
"I'm not even on the schedule today," he protested.
The union protested against the new shift pattern in writing.
She protested that she had been given no warning, and the file showed she was right.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun shifts the stress: /ˈproʊtɛst/, PROH-test
entries.русский: возражать, протестовать — с негодованием отвергать обвинение, и обычно неубедительно
entries.type: reporting verb — an indignant assertion made against an accusation
entries.patterns: protest + that-clause · protest + noun phrase (protest one's innocence; American also protest the ruling) · protest + to sb + that-clause · protest + against/at + noun phrase
entries.never: protest someone that, protest to do something, and protest someone something — ✗ He protested the guard that he had a pass, ✗ She protested to be innocent. Repairs: protested to the guard that he had a pass, protested that she was innocent.
entries.register note: American English lets protest take a direct object in the demonstration sense — students protested the tuition increase. British English requires protest against. Both standards keep against available; only American writing drops it freely.
entries.reports: asserting something in objection, almost always against a charge, and almost always with the implication that nobody is convinced. "I never touched it," he protested is a sentence in which the reader already suspects he did. Shakespeare's the lady doth protest too much turns on exactly this: too much denial reads as guilt.

examples: The site posted a document purporting to be an internal audit.
She produced a letter purporting to authorize the withdrawal.
The study purports to measure attention span, but it measures reaction time.
His purported resignation was never signed.
The caller purportedly worked for the county assessor's office.
Nothing in the archive purports to be a complete record.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun shifts the stress: /ˈpɜrpɔrt/, PUR-port
entries.русский: якобы являться, выдавать себя за — резкий маркер сомнения, особенно о документах
entries.type: reporting verb — a claim the writer strongly doubts
entries.patterns: purport + to-infinitive (the main and almost the only frame) · purport + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: purport someone to do something, purport + -ing, and purport + noun phrase. ✗ The memo purports the deal to be closed, ✗ purporting showing the transfer, ✗ He purported a degree in physics. Repairs: purports to show that the deal is closed, purporting to show the transfer, claimed a degree in physics.
entries.reports: what a thing presents itself as being, with the writer's clear suggestion that it may be nothing of the kind. It is the sharpest doubt marker available for documents, recordings, and objects: a memo purporting to show the transfer tells the reader the memo may well be a forgery. Human subjects are possible (he purports to be a licensed inspector) but the verb reaches its full force with inanimate ones. The adjective purported and adverb purportedly do the same job in a smaller space.

examples: The board reaffirmed its commitment to the scholarship fund.
She reaffirmed that no data had left the building.
The court reaffirmed a rule it had announced twenty years earlier.
Both governments reaffirmed the borders set out in the 1997 treaty.
He reaffirmed the timeline without offering any new evidence for it.
Nothing in the statement reaffirmed the original spending figure.
entries.русский: вновь подтверждать — официально повторять уже заявленную позицию
entries.type: reporting verb — a commitment restated on the record
entries.patterns: reaffirm + that-clause · reaffirm + noun phrase · reaffirm + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: reaffirm someone that and reaffirm to do something — ✗ He reaffirmed the allies that the guarantee held, ✗ She reaffirmed to support the treaty. Repairs: reaffirmed to the allies that the guarantee held, reaffirmed her support for the treaty.
entries.reports: stating again, formally, a position already taken — and the re- is doing real work, because the verb presupposes the earlier statement. Use it only where the reader knows or can infer what is being restated; he reaffirmed that the office opens at nine is odd unless somebody had raised a doubt. Compare reiterate, which carries impatience, and confirm, which answers a question rather than restating a promise.

examples: She reiterated that the offer would expire at midnight.
He reiterated the same three objections he had raised in June.
The chair reiterated to the room that questions would come at the end.
I'll reiterate it one last time so nobody can claim they weren't told.
The letter reiterates a demand the company has already refused twice.
Nothing was gained by reiterating a position everyone had already rejected.
entries.русский: повторять, вновь заявлять — с оттенком досады: с первого раза не услышали
entries.type: reporting verb — a statement repeated, usually because it was ignored
entries.patterns: reiterate + that-clause · reiterate + noun phrase · reiterate + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: reiterate someone that and reiterate to do something — ✗ He reiterated us that the deadline was Friday, ✗ She reiterated to check the figures. Repairs: reiterated to us that the deadline was Friday, repeated her instruction to check the figures.
entries.redundancy: reiterate again and reiterate once more say the same thing twice. The repetition is already inside the word; write reiterated or said again, not both.
entries.reports: saying again what has already been said, with a distinct note of impatience — the verb implies the first time did not take. It presupposes the earlier statement, like reaffirm, but where reaffirm is ceremonial and forward-looking, reiterate is corrective.

examples: The grant stipulates that the funds be spent within eighteen months.
Her father's will stipulated a trust for each grandchild.
The defense stipulated that the video was authentic.
The agreement stipulates that neither side discuss the terms publicly.
He stipulated only one condition: that his name stay off the building.
Nothing in the policy stipulates a maximum number of claims per year.
entries.русский: оговаривать, ставить условием; юр. признавать факт, не требуя его доказывания
entries.type: reporting verb — a condition laid down, or a fact agreed to
entries.patterns: stipulate + that-clause (subjunctive in the requirement sense, indicative in the agreement sense) · stipulate + noun phrase · stipulate + to + noun phrase (American legal: agree a fact need not be proved — stipulated to the chain of custody) · stipulate + for + noun phrase (rare, formal)
entries.never: stipulate someone to do something and stipulate someone that — ✗ The contract stipulated us to pay in advance, ✗ She stipulated the buyer that the roof was excluded. Repairs: stipulated that we pay in advance, stipulated that the roof was excluded.
entries.subjunctive: when stipulate lays down a requirement, the that-clause takes the bare subjunctive, exactly as after insist and demand — the lease stipulates that the deposit be paid before move-in, not that it is paid. When it reports an agreement about a fact, the clause is an ordinary indicative one and backshifts normally: the parties stipulated that the signature was genuine.
entries.reports: two related acts. In contracts, setting out a term that binds someone. In American courtrooms, agreeing that a fact need not be proved, which saves everyone the trouble of proving it — counsel stipulated to the chain of custody means nobody will argue about it.

examples: The spokesman stressed that the recall covered only one production run.
She stressed how quickly the situation could change.
He stressed the importance of getting the paperwork in early.
The doctor stressed to both parents that the fever was not dangerous.
Every version of the memo stressed confidentiality.
She stressed that she was speaking for herself and not for the department.
entries.русский: подчёркивать, акцентировать — то же, что emphasize, но короче; норма в новостях
entries.register: neutral; very common in news writing
entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.patterns: stress + that-clause · stress + noun phrase · stress + wh-clause · stress + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: stress someone that and stress to do something — ✗ She stressed me that the deadline was firm, ✗ He stressed to check the totals. Repairs: stressed to me that the deadline was firm, stressed the importance of checking the totals. Note that ✗ stress on is wrong for the same reason ✗ emphasize on is: the verb takes a plain object, the noun takes on (lay stress on the deadline).
entries.reports: the same act as emphasize, one syllable shorter, and for that reason the newsroom default. It is factive — he stressed that the vote was nonbinding commits the writer to the vote being nonbinding — and it implies no resistance, which is what separates it from insist.

examples: Counsel submits that the evidence was obtained without a warrant.
I submit that we have been solving the wrong problem for two years.
She submitted that the earlier reading of the statute could not survive.
He submitted, with respect, that the committee had exceeded its authority.
It is submitted that no other reading of the clause is available.
The paper submits a simpler explanation than the one currently accepted.
entries.русский: книжн./юр. осмелюсь утверждать — почтительно выдвигать тезис перед вышестоящей инстанцией
entries.type: reporting verb — a proposition advanced deferentially
entries.patterns: submit + that-clause · submit + to sb + that-clause (submitted to the court that…) · submit + noun phrase (submit a proposal, submit an explanation — put forward for consideration; also the everyday sense, hand in) · submit + to + noun phrase (a different sense: yield to)
entries.never: submit someone that and submit to do something in the assertion sense — ✗ Counsel submitted the court that the statute applied, ✗ He submitted to reverse the ruling. Repairs: submitted to the court that the statute applied, or simply submitted that the statute applied.
entries.reports: putting a proposition to somebody who has the authority to reject it. I submit that… is a hedge and a challenge at once: it defers in form while asserting in substance, which is why it belongs to advocates addressing a judge and scholars addressing a field. Outside those settings it sounds stiff or faintly pompous.

examples: He swore that the safe had been locked when he left.
She swore to tell the truth and then said almost nothing for an hour.
They swore us to secrecy before showing us the prototype.
I swear I put the keys on the hook.
He was sworn in as a judge on a Tuesday afternoon.
She'd swear to it in court if anyone asked her.
entries.русский: клясться, показывать под присягой — или разг. божиться: клянусь, я этого не делал
entries.type: reporting verb — a statement or promise made under oath, or with maximum personal warranty
entries.patterns: swear + that-clause · swear + to-infinitive · swear + to sb + that-clause · swear + sb + to + noun phrase (swore us to secrecy) · swear + sb + in (install by oath) · swear + to + noun phrase (swear to it) · swear + on + noun phrase · swear + at sb (a different sense: curse)
entries.never: swear someone that — ✗ He swore me that he'd been home. The addressee needs to: ✓ He swore to me that he'd been home. Also ✗ swear someone to do something meaning "promise them" — swear sb to binds the other person, as in sworn to secrecy.
entries.reports: asserting with the strongest personal guarantee available, either formally under oath (sworn testimony) or informally as an emphatic denial (I swear I didn't touch it). In legal settings the alternative is affirm, for witnesses who decline to take an oath. The curse sense — swear at someone — is a separate verb sharing the same form; the preposition tells them apart.

examples: Three former employees testified that the logs had been altered.
She testified before the subcommittee for nearly five hours.
He refused to testify against his own brother.
The expert testified to the reliability of the test.
She was subpoenaed but never actually testified.
Nothing he testified to at trial matched his earlier statement to police.
entries.русский: давать показания под присягой — свидетельствовать в суде; сам глагол нейтрален
entries.type: reporting verb — sworn statement given in a proceeding
entries.patterns: testify + that-clause · testify + to + noun phrase / -ing · testify + about/against/for + noun phrase · testify + before + noun phrase (testified before the committee)
entries.never: testify someone that, testify to do something, and testify to + a that-clause. ✗ She testified the jury that the door was open, ✗ He testified to be present, ✗ He testified to that the door was open. Repairs: testified that the door was open, testified to the door's being open, testified that he had been present.
entries.reports: giving evidence on the record, under oath, in a court or a hearing. The verb carries no stance of its own — it neither endorses nor doubts, because its whole point is the forum: what matters is that the statement was made where perjury is a crime. That neutrality is exactly why reporters use it. An inanimate subject shifts the sense to attest: the wreckage testifies to the force of the impact.

examples: She underlined that the arrangement was temporary.
The delay underlines how fragile the supply chain still is.
He underlined the words no exceptions twice in red ink.
Her resignation underlined the depth of the disagreement.
The report underlines a problem the board has known about for years.
Nothing in his answer underlined the urgency the memo had described.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun keeps the stress on the first syllable: /ˈʌndərlaɪn/, UN-der-lyne
entries.русский: подчёркивать — брит. вариант underscore; в амер. чаще о буквальном подчёркивании
entries.register: neutral, but British-leaning; American writing prefers underscore
entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.patterns: underline + that-clause · underline + noun phrase · underline + wh-clause · underline + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: underline someone that and underline to do something — ✗ He underlined us that the funding was temporary, ✗ She underlined to check the totals. Repairs: underlined to us that the funding was temporary, underlined the need to check the totals.
entries.reports: drawing attention to something already said, exactly as emphasize does, by the metaphor of a pen under a line of text. Both underline and underscore are current in American English, but American editors reach for underscore by a wide margin in the figurative sense and keep underline for what you literally do with a pen. Like the rest of the emphasis group it is factive.

examples: She underscored that the vote was advisory and nothing more.
The outage underscored how little redundancy the network had.
He underscored the importance of documenting every change.
The two resignations underscore a problem the board has ignored.
Her opening remarks underscored what the written report only implied.
Nothing in the briefing underscored the cost, which is what everyone wanted to hear about.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun keeps the stress on the first syllable: /ˈʌndərskɔr/, UN-der-skor
entries.русский: подчёркивать, акцентировать — амер. норма в переносном смысле, часто с неодуш. подлежащим
entries.register: neutral, journalistic; the standard American choice
entries.type: reporting verb — statement given extra weight
entries.patterns: underscore + that-clause · underscore + noun phrase · underscore + wh-clause · underscore + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: underscore someone that and underscore to do something — ✗ She underscored the committee that time was short, ✗ He underscored to move quickly. Repairs: underscored to the committee that time was short, underscored the need to move quickly.
entries.reports: the American twin of underline, and the more idiomatic of the two in figurative use. It works with a speaker (she underscored that the vote was advisory) but is especially at home with an inanimate subject, where an event rather than a person does the emphasizing: the outage underscored how little redundancy the system had. Factive, like the rest of the group.

examples: She vowed to appeal the ruling within the week.
He vowed that no one would be evicted while he was in office.
The company vowed revenge in the trade press and then quietly settled.
They exchanged vows in front of about forty people.
He vowed never to set foot in the building again.
Nobody who vowed to read the whole report actually did.
entries.русский: клятвенно обещать, зарекаться — личное торжественное обещание; ср. avow «признавать»
entries.type: reporting verb — a solemn personal promise
entries.patterns: vow + to-infinitive · vow + that-clause · vow + to sb + that-clause · vow + noun phrase (vowed revenge)
entries.never: vow someone to do something and vow someone that — ✗ He vowed us to return, ✗ She vowed me that she'd appeal. There is no indirect object: repairs are vowed to return, vowed to me that she would appeal, or promised me she would appeal.
entries.reports: a promise made with personal solemnity and, usually, some defiance. It is the headline writer's verb of choice because it is short and dramatic (Mayor vows to appeal), and it differs from pledge in being personal rather than institutional and from swear in requiring no oath. Do not confuse it with avow, which is an admission, not a promise.
